system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Compression or injury of the rostral dorsal midbrain/pretectal region near the superior colliculus disrupts vertical gaze circuitry and pretectal pupillary pathways. The characteristic syndrome includes impaired conjugate upgaze, convergence-retraction nystagmus, and pupillary light-near dissociation; pineal-region masses are a classic cause.
vignette: A 16-year-old boy has several weeks of worsening morning headaches, nausea, and blurred vision. MRI shows a pineal-region mass compressing the cerebral aqueduct. On examination, he cannot voluntarily look upward. Attempted upgaze produces jerky convergence and retraction of both eyes. The pupils constrict poorly to light but constrict normally during accommodation.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
distractor_notes: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia results from a medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion and causes impaired adduction of one eye with abducting nystagmus of the contralateral eye; it does not produce the classic upgaze palsy plus convergence-retraction nystagmus.

One-and-a-half syndrome combines a horizontal gaze palsy with ipsilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia from a pontine tegmental lesion. This patient instead has a dorsal midbrain vertical-gaze syndrome.
Weber syndrome is a ventral midbrain lesion producing ipsilateral oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiparesis. Those findings are absent here.
An Adie tonic pupil can show poor light reaction with relatively better near constriction, but it does not explain conjugate upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, or a pineal-region mass.
key_expl: The patient has Parinaud syndrome, also called dorsal midbrain syndrome. A pineal-region mass can compress the rostral midbrain/pretectum and cerebral aqueduct. The highly localizing combination is conjugate upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze, and pupillary light-near dissociation. The accompanying obstructive hydrocephalus explains the progressive morning headaches and nausea.
objective: Recognize Parinaud syndrome from a dorsal midbrain lesion causing impaired upgaze, convergence-retraction nystagmus, and light-near dissociation.
